source.title: Algebraic integers with conjugates in a prescribed distribution
source.version: arXiv:2111.12660v2, posted 16 March 2024, 47 pages, dated 19 March 2024 inside the file, with the arXiv comment '47 pages'; v1 is from 24 November 2021. summary: Complete extraction of the 47-page paper. Smith determines exactly which probability measures on a compact subset Σ of ℝ arise as weak* limits of the conjugate distributions of algebraic integers with all conjugates in Σ: when Σ has at most countably many components and capacity greater than 1, the only obstruction is that ∫ log|Q| dµ ≥ 0 for every nonzero integer polynomial Q, which is the integrality of resultants (Theorem 1.5). The converse implication was Serre's; the new content is that this necessary condition is sufficient, proved by combining the coefficient-adjustment technique of Robinson and of Fekete and Szegő with the geometry of numbers. The consequence is that Smyth's auxiliary-polynomial method computes the true constant in a whole class of optimisation problems (Theorem 5.11), and, applied to Serre's example, that the Schur–Siegel–Smyth constant satisfies λ_SSS < 1.89831 (Theorem 1.1), contradicting the long-standing expectation that it equals 2. Through Honda–Tate theory the same machinery gives F_q-simple abelian varieties with extreme point counts, improving the previous records. Of the 56 items, 3 are in the pinned libraries, 5 are planned by existing layers, and 48 are missing. The routing reflects the shape of the paper: the analytic core — logarithmic potential theory, capacity and equilibrium measures, Chebyshev polynomials of a compact set, the coefficient-adjustment and sweetening constructions, and the two main theorems — becomes a new roadmap, since a text search of every stage description in the atlas for 'capacity', 'equilibrium measure', 'logarithmic potential' and 'transfinite diameter' returns nothing at all. The two genuine geometry-of-numbers statements go to GeometryOfNumbersAndQuadraticArithmetic GN.1, the classical trace problem and Smyth's method to ClassicalArithmeticCompletion CA.6 with a polynomial-arithmetic lemma to CA.3, and Honda–Tate theory with the abelian-variety applications to FaltingsFinitenessAndIsogenyTheorems R28.4. No mistakes were found in the source: the numerics of Example 5.16 were recomputed and reproduce the paper's constants, and the cross-references and inequalities were checked. This is a paper inventory and routing, not a proof blueprint: the results quoted from Saff and Totik, Ransford, Fekete and Szegő, Robinson, Smyth, Serre, Honda and Tate, and Banaszczyk, Litvak, Pajor and Szarek are recorded as items with their own prerequisite entries and are not decomposed here.

items.name: Totally positive algebraic integers, the trace ratio and the constant λ_SSS
items.statement: For an algebraic integer α with conjugates α₁ = α, α₂, …, α_n, the degree is deg(α) = n and the trace is tr(α) = α₁ + ⋯ + α_n; α is totally positive if all its conjugates are positive reals. Define λ_SSS to be the least real number such that for every ε > 0 there are only finitely many totally positive algebraic integers α with tr(α) < (λ_SSS − ε)deg(α).
items.note: Schur proved e^{1/2} ≤ λ_SSS ≤ 2 in 1918, Siegel improved the lower bound to 1.7336 in 1945, Smyth to 1.7719 in 1984, and the state of the art before this paper was 1.793145 ≤ λ_SSS ≤ 2. ClassicalArithmeticCompletion CA.6, 'Special algebraic numbers and Mahler measure', plans the house, Mahler measure and the Pisot and Salem classes — the neighbouring family of special algebraic numbers, MSC 11R06 — but neither λ_SSS nor the notion of a totally positive algebraic integer appears anywhere in the atlas: a search of every stage description for 'trace problem', 'Smyth' and 'totally positive' finds only unrelated hits.

items.name: The Schur–Siegel–Smyth trace problem
items.statement: Fix ε > 0. Show that there are only finitely many totally positive algebraic integers α with tr(α) ≤ (2 − ε)deg(α), and explicitly compute the exceptions if possible. This is Borwein's codification of the problem, and reflects the general consensus that λ_SSS should equal 2.
items.note: The paper's Theorem 1.1 shows the consensus is wrong: λ_SSS < 1.89831. Not planned by any layer.

items.name: Smyth's auxiliary-polynomial method and the resultant argument
items.statement: Suppose for a given λ > 0 one has positive reals a₁, …, a_N and nonzero integer polynomials Q₁, …, Q_N with x ≥ λ + Σ_k a_k log|Q_k(x)| for all x > 0. Summing over the conjugates of a totally positive algebraic integer α whose minimal polynomial P is coprime to every Q_k, and using that ∏_{i≤n} Q_k(α_i) = res(P, Q_k) is a nonzero integer, gives tr(α) ≥ λ deg(α).
items.note: Smyth's original article realises this with λ = 1.7719 and about fifteen auxiliary polynomials; the state of the art uses 130 polynomials and λ = 1.793145. Smyth and Serre observed that there are λ < 2 for which no such inequality can hold; this was usually read as a limitation of the method, and the paper vindicates Smyth's opposite reading. Not planned; the integrality of the resultant is the only obstruction that survives (Theorem 1.5).

items.name: The Schur–Siegel–Smyth constant is less than 1.89831
items.statement: λ_SSS < 1.89831. In particular there are infinitely many totally positive algebraic integers α with tr(α) < 1.89831 · deg(α), so the expected value λ_SSS = 2 is wrong.
items.locator: arXiv:2111.12660v2 (16 March 2024), Theorem 1.1, p. 2; proved in Example 5.16, pp. 42–43
items.note: The constant is not optimal for two reasons recorded in Remark 1.2: the paper uses rounded forms of the optimal parameters for Serre's example, and even optimised Serre's argument cannot produce the true value of λ_SSS (Proposition 5.17). The proof applies the main theorem to an explicit measure built from Serre's two-part integration argument.

items.name: Extreme point counts for simple abelian varieties over finite fields
items.statement: There is C > 0 such that for every square prime power q ≥ C there are infinitely many F_q-simple abelian varieties A over F_q with #A(F_q) ≥ (q + 2√q − 0.89831)^{dim A} and infinitely many more with #A(F_q) ≤ (q − 2√q + 2.89831)^{dim A}.
items.locator: arXiv:2111.12660v2 (16 March 2024), Corollary 1.3, p. 3; deduced from Theorem 1.1 by Proposition 5.13
items.note: This improves the prior records. Further optimisation would sharpen the constants and extend the statement to non-square q, with constants depending on the fractional part of 2√q. The atlas has no layer on abelian varieties over finite fields: a search for 'Honda–Tate' and 'abelian varieties over finite fields' returns nothing.

items.name: Counting measures of polynomials and the weak* topology
items.statement: For α ∈ ℂ let δ_α be the Dirac measure. For a complex polynomial P(z) = a_n ∏_{i≤n}(z − α_i) of degree n ≥ 1, the counting measure is µ_P = (1/n)(δ_{α₁} + ⋯ + δ_{α_n}), a probability measure on the roots. For Σ ⊂ ℂ compact, the Borel measures supported in Σ carry the weak* topology: µ_k → µ if and only if ∫f dµ_k → ∫f dµ for every continuous f : Σ → ℝ. Throughout, 'measure' means a finite positive Borel measure on ℂ.
items.note: Borel measures, Dirac measures and weak convergence are in Mathlib in substantial part, and ArithmeticStatistics ST.0 plans 'Families, heights and measures' with the weak topologies used for equidistribution statements; the Tau Ceti optimal-transport roadmap plans weak* convergence of probability measures and Prokhorov-type compactness. The specific object µ_P is the paper's own and is used throughout.

items.name: The main theorem: which measures are limits of conjugate distributions
items.statement: Let Σ be a compact subset of ℝ with at most countably many connected components and capacity strictly greater than 1, and let µ be a Borel probability measure with support in Σ. Then the following are equivalent: (1) ∫_Σ log|Q(x)| dµ(x) ≥ 0 for every nonzero integer polynomial Q; (2) there is an infinite sequence of distinct irreducible monic integer polynomials R₁, R₂, … with supp(µ_{R_k}) ⊆ Σ for every k and µ_{R_k} → µ in the weak* topology.
items.note: The implication (2) ⇒ (1) is Serre's, and follows from the upper semicontinuity of log|Q| together with log|res(R_k, Q)| ≥ 0. The converse is the new content and occupies most of the paper: the only obstruction to realising a measure as a limit of conjugate distributions is the integrality of resultants, which is exactly Smyth's method. The restriction to countably many components is probably necessary — there are totally disconnected compact subsets of ℝ of capacity greater than 1 containing no algebraic number — while the restriction to Σ ⊂ ℝ and to capacity > 1 is expected to be removable, the capacity-1 case reducing by Proposition 5.7 to the unweighted equilibrium measure and being known only in special cases.

items.name: Logarithmic potential, energy, capacity and the equilibrium measure
items.statement: For Σ ⊂ ℂ compact and µ a Borel measure on Σ, the potential function is U^µ(z) = ∫_Σ −log|z − w| dµ(w) and the energy is I(µ) = ∫_Σ U^µ dµ ∈ ℝ ∪ {∞}. The capacity of Σ is κ_Σ = sup_µ e^{−I(µ)} over probability measures supported in Σ. If κ_Σ > 0 the supremum is attained by a unique probability measure of minimal energy, the unweighted equilibrium measure µ_Σ of Σ.
items.note: The foundational notions of logarithmic potential theory, equivalently the transfinite diameter and Chebyshev constant of a compact set. They appear nowhere in the atlas: a search of every stage description for 'capacity', 'equilibrium measure', 'logarithmic potential' and 'transfinite diameter' returns nothing, and the single hit for 'potential theory' is the Tau Ceti PDE roadmap's lane on maximum principles and harmonic functions, which is a different subject.

items.name: Hölder measures
items.statement: A Borel measure µ on ℝ is η-Hölder for η > 0 if there is C > 0 with µ([x, y]) ≤ C(y − x)^η for all x < y; µ is Hölder if it is η-Hölder for some η > 0.
items.note: The regularity class in which almost all of the paper works. It is exactly what makes the potential function continuous (Lemma 2.3) and the layer-cake identity (2.2) effective.

items.name: Potentials of Hölder measures are Hölder continuous
items.statement: For η ∈ (0,1) and µ an η-Hölder measure supported in a compact subset of ℝ, the potential U^µ is a finite, η-Hölder continuous function on ℝ: there is C > 0 with |U^µ(y) − U^µ(x)| ≤ C|y − x|^η for all x, y.
items.locator: arXiv:2111.12660v2 (16 March 2024), Lemma 2.3, p. 6, using the layer-cake identity (2.2) and Tonelli's theorem
items.note: The identity ∫_I log|x − t| dµ(t) = log b · µ(I) − ∫₀^b r^{-1} µ([x−r, x+r] ∩ I) dr for I ⊆ [x−b, x+b] is where the Hölder condition enters, and it recurs throughout §§2–4.

items.name: Compact finite unions of intervals
items.statement: A compact Σ ⊂ ℝ is a compact finite union of intervals if it is nonempty, has finitely many connected components and has no isolated points.
items.note: The class of sets to which the hard part of the proof is reduced by Proposition 2.5.

items.name: Reduction to Hölder measures on compact finite unions of intervals
items.statement: Let Σ ⊂ ℝ be compact with at most countably many components and capacity > 1, and let µ be a probability measure on Σ satisfying condition (1) of Theorem 1.5. Then there are Hölder probability measures µ₁, µ₂, … and closed subsets Σ₁, Σ₂, … of Σ such that each Σ_k is a compact finite union of intervals containing supp(µ_k), each µ_k satisfies ∫_{Σ_k} log|Q| dµ_k ≥ 0 for every nonzero integer polynomial Q, and µ_k → µ weak*.
items.locator: arXiv:2111.12660v2 (16 March 2024), Proposition 2.5, p. 7; proved in §5
items.note: The reduction that makes the rest of the argument possible; its proof uses the convolution and sweetening constructions of §5.

items.name: The weight w_µ and the n-norm
items.statement: For a Hölder measure µ supported in a compact Σ ⊂ ℝ, the weight is w_µ(z) = exp(U^µ(z)) ∈ ℝ_{>0} ∪ {∞}. For a complex polynomial P and n ≥ 0, the n-norm of P with respect to (µ, Σ) is ‖w_µ^n P‖_Σ = max_{x ∈ Σ} (w_µ(x)^n |P(x)|).
items.note: The weighted supremum norm of weighted potential theory. Everything in §§3–4 is an estimate for such norms; the target is to produce integer polynomials whose n-norm grows subexponentially.

items.name: A criterion for weak* convergence of counting measures
items.statement: Let Σ ⊂ ℝ be compact and µ a Hölder probability measure on Σ. Let P₁, P₂, … be real monic polynomials of increasing degree with all roots in Σ, and suppose ‖w_µ^{deg P_n} P_n‖_Σ^{1/deg P_n} → 1. Then µ_{P₁}, µ_{P₂}, … converge to µ in the weak* topology on Σ.
items.note: The bridge from the norm estimates to the statement of Theorem 1.5: it is the last step of the proof in §4.1.

items.name: Removing a root changes the n-norm by a polynomial factor
items.statement: Let Σ be a compact finite union of intervals and µ a Hölder probability measure on Σ. There is C > 0 depending on Σ and µ such that for all n ≥ 0, m ≥ 1, every complex polynomial P of degree m and every root α of P, the polynomial Q(z) = P(z)/(z − α) satisfies ‖w_µ^n Q‖_Σ ≤ (2·max(n,m))^C ‖w_µ^n P‖_Σ.
items.note: A workhorse estimate used in §3 to pass between a polynomial and its cofactors, and in the proof of Lemma 3.8.

items.name: The gcd of integer polynomials and primitivity
items.statement: For nonzero integer polynomials Q₁, …, Q_k, gcd(Q₁,…,Q_k) is the unique integer polynomial G of maximal degree with positive leading term, primitive coefficients, and dividing each Q_i in ℚ[z]; by Gauss's lemma each Q_i/G is an integer polynomial.
items.note: Gauss's lemma and primitive polynomials are in Mathlib (`Polynomial.IsPrimitive`, `Polynomial.IsPrimitive.Int.dvd_iff_map_cast_dvd_map_cast` and the `IsIntegrallyClosed`/`UFD` content-and-primitive-part API), and CA.3 plans the surrounding integer-polynomial arithmetic. The particular normalisation used here is the paper's own bookkeeping.

items.name: A squarefree integral combination of integer polynomials
items.statement: Let k ≥ 1, n ≥ 0 and let Q₁, …, Q_k be nonzero integer polynomials of degree at most n with some Q_i of degree exactly n, and put G = gcd(Q₁,…,Q_k). Then there are nonnegative integers b₂, …, b_k, each at most 2(n − deg G), such that (Q₁ + b₂Q₂ + ⋯ + b_kQ_k)/G is squarefree of degree n − deg G.
items.note: A purely polynomial-arithmetic statement: a generic small integral combination of polynomials with a common factor removed is squarefree. It is used in the proof of Theorem 3.1 to produce the squarefree integer polynomial the geometry of numbers then adjusts. CA.3 plans integer-polynomial arithmetic with resultants and discriminants, and is the natural owner, but does not state this.

items.name: The approximating polynomial of a measure
items.statement: For Σ ⊂ ℝ compact, µ a Hölder probability measure on Σ and n ≥ 1, let α_i be the least α ∈ Σ with µ((−∞, α]) = i/n for 0 ≤ i ≤ n, and set P_{n,µ}(z) = ∏_{i=1}^n (z − α_i). Then −n^{-1} ≤ (µ_{P_{n,µ}} − µ)((−∞, x]) ≤ 0 for all x, so |(µ_{P_{n,µ}} − µ)(I)| ≤ n^{-1} for every closed interval I.
items.note: The quantile discretisation of µ, whose roots are the nodes at which all later interpolation and evaluation arguments take place.

items.name: Discriminant and weight estimates for the approximating polynomial
items.statement: Let Σ ⊂ ℝ be compact and µ a Hölder probability measure on Σ. There is C > 0 determined by Σ and µ so that for all n ≥ 2, with α₁, …, α_n and P_{n,µ} as above, n^{−Cn} exp(−½n²I(µ)) ≤ ∏_{1≤i<j≤n} |α_i − α_j|, and, setting ρ_{n,µ}(x) = min_i |x − α_i|, one has n^{−C}ρ_{n,µ}(x) ≤ w_µ(x)^n |P_{n,µ}(x)| ≤ n^C ρ_{n,µ}(x) for all x ∈ Σ.
items.locator: arXiv:2111.12660v2 (16 March 2024), Proposition 2.12, p. 10, equations (2.7) and (2.8)
items.note: The quantitative link between the energy of µ and the Vandermonde determinant of the discretisation; it is what converts potential-theoretic information into the determinant bound that the geometry of numbers consumes.

items.name: Existence of squarefree integer polynomials of small weighted norm
items.statement: Let Σ ⊂ ℝ be compact and µ a Hölder probability measure on Σ with ∫ log|Q| dµ ≥ 0 for every nonzero integer polynomial Q. Then there is C > 0 determined by µ and Σ such that for every n ≥ 2 there is a squarefree integer polynomial R_n of degree n with ‖w_µ^n R_n‖_Σ ≤ n^{C√n}.
items.note: The first main output of the geometry-of-numbers section, proved from Proposition 3.6, Lemma 3.8 and Lemma 2.10 by an extremal argument over the gcd degrees m_k. It supplies the squarefree modulus for the coefficient adjustment of Corollary 3.3.

items.name: A flatness-theorem estimate for integer polynomials
items.statement: There is C > 0 such that: given positive integers c, n and a squarefree integer polynomial Q(z) = c(z − α₁)⋯(z − α_n) with the α_i distinct, writing Q_i(z) = Q(z)/(z − α_i), every real polynomial P of degree at most n − 1 admits complex numbers β₁, …, β_n with Σ_i |β_i| ≤ Cn log 2n such that P(z) − Σ_i β_i Q_i(z) is an integer polynomial.
items.note: An application of the flatness theorem of the geometry of numbers: the lattice of integer polynomials is not far from any real polynomial in the basis dual to evaluation at the roots of Q. GeometryOfNumbersAndQuadraticArithmetic GN.1 plans the Blichfeldt and Minkowski convex-body and successive-minima theorems, but a search of every stage description for 'flatness theorem', 'covering radius' and 'successive minima' outside GN.1's own title finds nothing, and this statement is not planned.

items.name: Approximating a real polynomial by an integer polynomial in the weighted norm
items.statement: Let Σ be a compact finite union of intervals and µ a Hölder probability measure on Σ. For n > 1, a real polynomial P of degree at most n − 1 and a squarefree integer polynomial Q of degree n, there is an integer polynomial R of degree at most n − 1 with ‖w_µ^n(P − R)‖_Σ ≤ n^C ‖w_µ^n Q‖_Σ, where C > 0 depends only on Σ and µ.
items.note: The coefficient-adjustment step in its final form: Theorem 3.2 makes P congruent to an integer polynomial modulo the lattice spanned by the Q_i, and Lemma 2.8 bounds the resulting error by the norm of Q.

items.name: A product bound for successive minima of evaluation polytopes
items.statement: Let m ≥ 0, let α₁, …, α_{m+1} be distinct reals and v₁, …, v_{m+1} positive reals, and let K be the set of real polynomials P of degree at most m with v_i|P(α_i)| ≤ 1 for all i. For 0 ≤ i ≤ m let λ_i be the least real with λ_iK containing i + 1 linearly independent integer polynomials. Then D/(m+1)! ≤ λ₀λ₁⋯λ_m ≤ D, where D = ∏_i v_i · ∏_{i<j} |α_i − α_j|.
items.note: Minkowski's second theorem applied to the convex body cut out by weighted evaluation conditions, with the Vandermonde determinant computing the covolume. It is the engine of §3 and, like Theorem 3.2, belongs to the geometry-of-numbers layer GN.1 rather than to potential theory.

items.name: A lower bound for products of weighted norms
items.statement: Let µ be a Hölder probability measure on a compact Σ ⊂ ℝ, let n, m ≥ 0, let R be a nonzero integer polynomial and let Q₀, …, Q_m be linearly independent integer polynomials of degree at most m. If ∫_Σ log|R| dµ ≥ 0, then ∏_{i=0}^m ‖w_µ^n Q_iR‖_Σ ≥ (1/(m+1)!) exp((mn − ½m² + n − ½m)I(µ)).
items.note: The lower half of the extremal estimate, obtained from Proposition 3.4 with v_k = |(R·Q_k)(α_k)|^{-1}.

items.name: Near-sharpness of the product bound
items.statement: Let Σ be a compact finite union of intervals, µ a Hölder probability measure on Σ and n ≥ 2. Then there are linearly independent integer polynomials Q₀, …, Q_n of degree at most n with ∏_{i=0}^n ‖w_µ^n Q_i‖_Σ ≤ n^{Cn} exp(½n²I(µ)), where C > 0 depends only on µ and Σ.
items.note: The matching upper bound, proved by applying Proposition 3.4 to the nodes of the approximating polynomial with v_k = |P_k(α_k)|^{-1} and using Proposition 2.12 and Lemma 2.8 to control the resulting norms.

items.name: Nonpositivity of the energy of an admissible Hölder measure
items.statement: Let µ be a Hölder probability measure on a compact Σ ⊂ ℝ with ∫_Σ log|Q| dµ ≥ 0 for every nonzero integer polynomial Q. Then I(µ) ≤ 0.
items.note: The paper describes this as the statement that accounts for the discriminant of a squarefree integer polynomial being a nonzero integer. It is generalised to arbitrary Borel measures in Proposition 5.7, which is what the reduction of Proposition 2.5 needs.

items.name: The gcd-refined lower bound for products of weighted norms
items.statement: Let µ be a Hölder probability measure on a compact finite union of intervals Σ. There is C > 0 such that for 0 ≤ k ≤ m ≤ n with n ≥ 2 and linearly independent integer polynomials Q₀, …, Q_m of degree at most n with ‖w_µ^n Q₀‖_Σ ≤ ⋯ ≤ ‖w_µ^n Q_m‖_Σ, setting G = gcd(Q₀,…,Q_k) and assuming ∫_Σ log|G| dµ ≥ 0 and m = max_{i≤k} deg(Q_i/G), one has ∏_{i=0}^m ‖w_µ^n Q_i‖_Σ ≥ n^{−Cn} exp((mn − ½m²)I(µ)).
items.note: Combines Theorem 3.2 and Proposition 3.5: the auxiliary polynomials H_j built from Theorem 3.2 applied to ½z^j are linearly independent because their images in F₂[z] are, which supplies the missing directions in the lattice.

items.name: The key construction: real polynomials with many integral coefficients
items.statement: Let Σ be a compact finite union of intervals of capacity κ > 1, µ a Hölder probability measure on Σ and B > 0. There is C > 3 depending on Σ, µ, B such that for every integer n > C, setting m = ⌊B√n log n⌋, there is a real monic polynomial P_n of degree n which (1) is squarefree with all roots in Σ, (2) satisfies ‖w_µ^{n−m}P_n‖_Σ ≤ n^Cκ^m, (3) has even integer coefficients in every degree k ∈ [n−m, n−1], and (4) has roots α₁ < ⋯ < α_n admitting x₁ < α₁ < y₁ < ⋯ < x_n < α_n < y_n with [x_k, y_k] ⊆ Σ and min(w_µ(x_k)^{n−m}|P_n(x_k)|, w_µ(y_k)^{n−m}|P_n(y_k)|) ≥ n^{−C}κ^m.
items.locator: arXiv:2111.12660v2 (16 March 2024), Proposition 4.1, p. 21, equations (4.1) and (4.2)
items.note: The technical heart of the paper. Given it, Theorem 1.5 follows in §4.1: split P_n into its top m + 1 coefficients, which are already even integers, and a real tail; use Theorem 3.1 and Corollary 3.3 to replace the tail by 4R(z) − 2 for an integer polynomial R; the resulting monic integer polynomial R_n is within the margin (4.2) of P_n at every x_k and y_k, so it has one root in each [x_k, y_k] and no others, it is irreducible by Eisenstein at 2, and ‖w_µ^n R_n‖_Σ^{1/n} → 1, so Lemma 2.7 applies.

items.name: Chebyshev polynomials of a compact set
items.statement: For r ≥ 0 there is a unique real monic polynomial T_r of degree r for which there are r + 1 points x₀ < ⋯ < x_r in Σ with (−1)^{r−i}T_r(x_i) = ‖T_r‖_Σ for all i; it satisfies C^{-1}κ^r ≤ ‖T_r‖_Σ ≤ Cκ^r with C > 1 depending only on Σ, where κ is the capacity.
items.note: The classical equioscillation characterisation of Chebyshev polynomials of a compact set, together with the identification of the limit of ‖T_r‖_Σ^{1/r} with the capacity. The atlas has Chebyshev polynomials only as an orthogonal basis of L²([−1,1]) in the Tau Ceti completed roadmap on orthogonal bases, which is a different object and does not give these bounds.

items.name: Pruned polynomials
items.statement: For n ≥ 1 and P a real monic squarefree polynomial with root set S, suppose there is a subset S̃ ⊆ S ∩ Σ of cardinality n such that for every connected component I of Σ meeting S, the set I ∩ S̃ contains neither the least nor the greatest element of I ∩ S. Then ∏_{α ∈ S̃}(z − α) is a degree n pruned polynomial of P.
items.note: The device for discarding the roots nearest the ends of each component of Σ, where the equioscillation control degrades.

items.name: A modified Chebyshev polynomial with a controlled sign pattern
items.statement: There is C > 0 depending only on Σ such that for every r ≥ 2 there are a real monic polynomial T̃_r of degree r with ‖T̃_r‖_Σ ≤ r^Cκ^r, an integer k₁ ≤ k₀, and reals y₁ < ⋯ < y_{r+k₁} in Σ with |T̃_r(y_i)| ≥ C^{-1}κ^r for all i, such that (y₁, y_{r+k₁}) contains all the roots of T̃_r and each (y_i, y_{i+1}) either does not lie in Σ and contains no root of T̃_r, or lies in Σ and contains exactly one root.
items.note: Here k₀ is the number of connected components of Σ; the proof compares T̃_r with T_{r+3k₀}. This is the polynomial along which the coefficient adjustment is performed.

items.name: The coefficient-adjustment lemma of Robinson and Fekete–Szegő
items.statement: Let P be a monic real polynomial of degree n and r ≥ 2, with y₁ < ⋯ < y_{r+k₁} constructed from T̃_r as in Lemma 4.4. Then there is a monic real polynomial T of degree r such that the degree i coefficient of T^D P is an even integer for every i ∈ [(D−1)r + n, Dr + n − 1], and |T(y_i)/T̃_r(y_i)| ≥ 1/2 for all i, with ‖T‖_Σ ≤ r^{C₁}κ^r + 2C₁rκ^r.
items.note: The technique goes back to Robinson and to Fekete and Szegő, Theorem D: one adjusts the top coefficients of a power of an auxiliary polynomial to be integral while keeping its size under control. Here D = ⌈4C₁²/(κ−1)⌉ is fixed once Lemmas 4.2 and 4.4 hold with C = C₁.

items.name: Complementary polynomials
items.statement: Given Σ, κ, C₁, D as above, a real monic P of degree n and r ≥ 2, take T from Lemma 4.5 and set Q₀(x) = ∏_{j=0}^{D−1}(T(x) − ((2j+1)/(4DC₁))κ^r). With d = rD − r, choose ε_d, …, ε₁ ≥ 0 minimal in turn so that (Q₀ + ε_dT_d + ⋯ + ε_iT_i)·P has an even coefficient in degree d + n + 1 − (d − i + 1), and put Q = Q₀ + ε_dT_d + ⋯ + ε₁T₁ + N with N ≥ 0 minimal so that |Q(α)| ≥ n^{-1}C₂^{-1}κ^{Dr} at every root α of P, where C₂ = 8(4DC₁)^D. This Q is the complementary polynomial to P of degree Dr, and every coefficient of PQ in the relevant range is an even integer.
items.locator: arXiv:2111.12660v2 (16 March 2024), Definition 4.6, pp. 25–26, equations (4.7) and (4.8)
items.note: The construction that produces, from an arbitrary monic real polynomial, a partner making the product have a long block of even integer coefficients while keeping all roots in Σ.

items.name: Complementary polynomials are squarefree with well-separated roots in Σ
items.statement: There is C > 1 such that for r ≥ C, n ≥ 0 and P real monic of degree n with complementary polynomial Q of degree Dr: Q is squarefree with all roots in Σ, and every root β of Q lies in an interval [x, y] ⊆ Σ containing no other root of Q with |Q(x)|, |Q(y)| ≥ C^{-1}κ^{Dr} (Lemma 4.7). Moreover ‖Q‖_Σ ≤ r^Cκ^{Dr} and ‖Q′‖_Σ ≤ r^Cκ^{Dr}, and for every root β, |Q(x)| ≥ C^{-1}κ^{Dr}|x − β| for x ∈ [β − r^{-C}, β + r^{-C}] (Lemma 4.8).
items.locator: arXiv:2111.12660v2 (16 March 2024), Lemmas 4.7 and 4.8, pp. 26–28, equation (4.11)
items.note: The two estimates that make condition (4) of Proposition 4.1 available for the complementary factor.

items.name: Well-separated approximating polynomials
items.statement: With Σ and µ fixed and d an integer, there is C > 0 such that for every n ≥ 2 there is a monic squarefree polynomial P̃_n of degree n with: every root α having [α − n^{-C}, α + n^{-C}] ⊆ Σ and containing no other root; w_µ^{n+d}(x)|P̃_n(x)| ≥ n^{-C} min_α|x − α| for all x ∈ Σ; and ‖w_µ^{n+d}P̃_n‖_Σ ≤ n^C.
items.note: A pruned and perturbed form of the approximating polynomial of Definition 2.11, and the other factor of P_n = P̃_{n−Dr}Q_{Dr} in the proof of Proposition 4.1.

items.name: The measure ν_[a,b] and its potential
items.statement: For b > a > 0 let ν_{[a,b]} be the measure on [a,b] with dν_{[a,b]}(t) = √(ab) dt/(πt√((b−t)(t−a))). It is a 1/2-Hölder probability measure, U^{ν_{[a,b]}}(z) + log|z| − log((a + 2√(ab) + b)/(b−a)) vanishes for z ∈ [a,b] and is ≤ 0 otherwise, and U^{ν_{[a,b]}}(0) = log((a + 2√(ab) + b)/(4ab)).
items.locator: arXiv:2111.12660v2 (16 March 2024), Notation 5.1 and Lemma 5.2, pp. 31–32, equation (5.1)
items.note: The pushforward under z ↦ 1/z of the equilibrium measure of [b^{-1}, a^{-1}], and the second of the two measures in Serre's argument; it is also the smoothing kernel used in Notation 5.3.

items.name: Smoothing by convolution and its effect on potentials
items.statement: For ε ∈ (0, 1/2) put ν_ε = ν_{[ε², ε]}. For a Borel measure µ on a compact Σ ⊂ ℝ, the convolution µ * ν_ε is 1/2-Hölder with support in {x : [x − ε, x − ε²] ∩ Σ ≠ ∅}, and U^{µ*ν_ε}(z) − U^µ(z) ≤ log((ε² + 2ε^{3/2} + ε)/(ε − ε²)) ≤ Cε^{1/2} uniformly in z, ε and µ. If µ * ν_ε is supported in Σ for all small ε, then µ * ν_ε → µ weak* as ε → 0.
items.locator: arXiv:2111.12660v2 (16 March 2024), Notation 5.3 and Lemma 5.4, p. 33, equation (5.5)
items.note: The regularisation that turns an arbitrary admissible measure into a Hölder one at a controlled cost in potential, which is half of Proposition 2.5.

items.name: Sweetened measures
items.statement: Let Σ ⊂ ℝ be compact of capacity κ > 1, Σ′ ⊇ Σ compact, µ a probability measure and ν a measure on Σ′ with γ = 1 − ν(Σ′) ∈ [0,1]. Let µ_Σ be the unweighted equilibrium measure of Σ and B = sup_{U^µ(z)<∞}(U^{ν+γµ_Σ}(z) − U^µ(z)), assumed finite; then B ≥ 0. The sweetened measure of ν with respect to Σ and µ is sw(ν) = (β + γ − βγ)µ_Σ + (1−β)ν, where β ∈ [0,1) satisfies β/(1−β) = B/log κ; β + γ − βγ is the measure of sweetener. It satisfies U^{sw(ν)}(z) ≤ (1−β)U^µ(z) for all z.
items.locator: arXiv:2111.12660v2 (16 March 2024), Definition 5.5, pp. 34–35, equations (5.7) and (5.8)
items.note: The device that restores the admissibility condition after smoothing, by adding a controlled amount of equilibrium measure. Remark 5.6 records that for Σ = [x₁,y₁] ∪ ⋯ ∪ [x_k,y_k] the equilibrium measure has density |P(t)|∏_i|t−x_i|^{-1/2}|t−y_i|^{-1/2} for a polynomial P, so it is 1/2-Hölder and sweetening preserves the Hölder condition.

items.name: Nonpositivity of the energy in general
items.statement: Let µ be a Borel probability measure with support in a compact subset of ℝ such that ∫ log|Q| dµ ≥ 0 for every nonzero integer polynomial Q. Then I(µ) ≤ 0.
items.note: The removal of the Hölder hypothesis from Corollary 3.7, proved by smoothing and sweetening inside a long interval. It is what shows that at capacity exactly 1 the only candidate measure is the unweighted equilibrium measure.

items.name: The optimisation constants λ(Σ, F) and λ_Smyth(Σ, F)
items.statement: Let Σ ⊆ ℝ be closed with at most countably many components and capacity > 1, and F : Σ → ℝ continuous with F(x_i)/log|x_i| → +∞ along any sequence with |x_i| → ∞ when Σ is unbounded. Enumerating the algebraic integers α_i all of whose conjugates lie in Σ, with degrees n_i and minimal polynomials P_i, set λ(Σ,F) = liminf_i ∫_Σ F dµ_{P_i}. Let λ_Smyth(Σ,F) be the least upper bound of the λ for which there are nonzero integer polynomials Q₁,…,Q_N and positive a₁,…,a_N with F(x) ≥ λ + Σ_i a_i log|Q_i(x)| for all x ∈ Σ.
items.locator: arXiv:2111.12660v2 (16 March 2024), Notation 5.8 and Theorem 5.11, pp. 37 and 39, equations (5.11) and (5.15)
items.note: Example 5.9 records that F(x) = x and Σ = ℝ_{≥0} give λ(Σ,F) = λ_SSS, so the trace problem is the model case of this class of optimisation problems.

items.name: Reduction of the optimisation to a compact subset
items.statement: Given Σ and F as above, there is a compact Σ₀ ⊆ Σ such that for every probability measure µ with compact support in Σ but not in Σ₀ there is a probability measure µ′ supported in Σ₀ with ∫F dµ > ∫F dµ′ and with ∫log|Q| dµ′ ≥ 0 for every integer polynomial Q with ∫log|Q| dµ ≥ 0.
items.note: The step that handles unbounded Σ, using the growth condition (5.11) on F.

items.name: Smyth's method computes the optimum
items.statement: For Σ and F as in Notation 5.8, λ(Σ, F) = λ_Smyth(Σ, F).
items.note: The vindication of Smyth's method: the auxiliary-polynomial inequalities capture the true constant, so the apparent limitations of the method observed by Smyth and Serre are in fact limitations of the constant. Combined with Serre's example (Example 5.16), which shows no such inequality can hold for λ > 1.89830…, this proves Theorem 1.1.

items.name: Point counts of abelian varieties over a finite field in terms of λ(Σ, F)
items.statement: Let q be a prime power, Σ = [−2√q, 2√q] and F(x) = log|q + 1 − x|. Then for every ε > 0 there are infinitely many F_q-simple abelian varieties A over F_q with #A(F_q)^{1/dim A} ≤ exp(λ(Σ,F) + ε), infinitely many more with #A(F_q)^{1/dim A} ≥ exp(−λ(Σ,−F) − ε), and only finitely many with #A(F_q)^{1/dim A} outside [exp(λ(Σ,F) − ε), exp(−λ(Σ,−F) + ε)].
items.note: The reduction, by Honda–Tate theory, of extreme point counts for abelian varieties over finite fields to an optimisation problem of the same shape as the trace problem: the Frobenius eigenvalues of a simple abelian variety are the conjugates of a Weil q-number, and for real Weil numbers these lie in [−2√q, 2√q]. Remark 5.14 adds that the congruence freedom in the construction of the R_k modulo 4q lets the families be taken geometrically simple and ordinary.

items.name: Explicit point-count bounds from the trace constant
items.statement: With λ_SSS as in Example 5.9 and any ε > 0, there is C > 0 such that for every square prime power q > C there are infinitely many F_q-simple abelian varieties with #A(F_q) ≥ (q + 2√q + 1 − λ_SSS − ε)^{dim A} and infinitely many more with #A(F_q) ≤ (q − 2√q + 1 + λ_SSS + ε)^{dim A}.
items.note: With Theorem 1.1 this gives Corollary 1.3. The link between the two optimisation problems is that near the endpoints of [−2√q, 2√q] the function log|q + 1 − x| is, after rescaling, the trace functional.

items.name: A sufficient criterion for admissibility via potentials
items.statement: Let Σ ⊂ ℝ be compact of capacity > 1 with at most countably many components and µ a probability measure on Σ. Suppose there are distinct irreducible primitive integer polynomials Q₁, …, Q_N and positive reals a₁, …, a_N with Σ_i a_i deg Q_i ≤ 1 and U^µ(z) ≤ −Σ_i a_i log|Q_i(z)| for all z ∈ ℂ, and suppose ∫_Σ log|Q_i| dµ ≥ 0 for each i. Then µ satisfies the equivalent conditions of Theorem 1.5.
items.note: The practical criterion by which a candidate measure is certified; it is how Example 5.16 verifies the hypotheses of Theorem 1.5 for Serre's measure.

items.name: Serre's measure and the proof of Theorem 1.1
items.statement: Take a = 0.087353, b = 4.411076, γ = 0.215485 and µ = γν_{[a,b]} + (1−γ)µ_{[a,b]}, where µ_{[a,b]} is the unweighted equilibrium measure of [a,b]. Then U^µ(z) + γ log|z| equals a constant C ≈ −1.3·10^{−7} on [a,b] and is at most C elsewhere, ∫log|x| dµ(x) ≈ 1.5·10^{−6} is nonnegative, so Proposition 5.15 applies with Q₁(z) = z; and ∫x dµ(x) = γ√(ab) + (1−γ)(a+b)/2 ∈ (1.898303, 1.898304). Applying Theorem 1.5 to µ proves Theorem 1.1.
items.note: The measure repackages, as a single convex combination, Serre's two-part argument in a letter to Smyth, which integrated the auxiliary inequality first against µ_{[a,b]} and then against the pushforward of the equilibrium measure of [b^{-1}, a^{-1}] under z ↦ 1/z — the latter being ν_{[a,b]}. The parameters a and b are rounded forms of the optimal ones.

items.name: Finitely many auxiliary polynomials never suffice
items.statement: Let Σ and F be as in Notation 5.8, let µ be a probability measure with compact support in Σ with ∫log|Q| dµ ≥ 0 for every nonzero integer polynomial Q and ∫F dµ = λ(Σ,F), and let P be an irreducible monic nonconstant integer polynomial with ∫_Σ F dµ_P < λ(Σ,F) whose roots lie in an open subset of ℝ contained in Σ. Then ∫_Σ log|P| dµ = 0 and the supports of µ_P and µ are disjoint.
items.note: The obstruction explaining Remark 1.2: an optimal measure must be orthogonal to every such P, so Serre's one-polynomial argument cannot produce λ_SSS, and the optimisation problems grow in complexity with the number of auxiliary polynomials.

items.name: Algebraic integers, conjugates, minimal polynomials and resultants
items.statement: The minimal polynomial of an algebraic integer over ℚ, its complex roots (the conjugates), and the resultant res(P, Q) = ∏_i Q(α_i) of two polynomials, which is a nonzero integer when P and Q are coprime integer polynomials with P monic.
items.note: Mathlib has algebraic integers, minimal polynomials and resultants in substantial part, and CA.3 plans the integer-polynomial arithmetic — 'integer-valued polynomials, irreducibility, resultants, discriminants' — while the Tau Ceti number-field arithmetic and polynomial Galois roadmaps plan conjugates and discriminants. The identity ∏_i Q(α_i) = res(P, Q) and its integrality are exactly what Smyth's method uses.

items.name: Eisenstein's criterion
items.statement: A monic integer polynomial whose non-leading coefficients are divisible by a prime p and whose constant term is not divisible by p² is irreducible over ℚ.
items.locator: arXiv:2111.12660v2 (16 March 2024), used in §4.1, p. 22, at the prime 2
items.note: The polynomials R_n constructed in §4.1 have the form z^n + ⋯ + 4R(z) − 2, so they are Eisenstein at 2; this is what makes them irreducible and hence minimal polynomials of algebraic integers. Mathlib has Eisenstein's criterion.

items.name: Tonelli's theorem and the monotone convergence theorem
items.statement: Tonelli's theorem for nonnegative measurable functions on a product of σ-finite measure spaces, and the monotone convergence theorem, used for the layer-cake identity (2.2) and for passing to the limit against the upper semicontinuous function log|Q|.
items.note: Both are in Mathlib's measure theory library, with the product-measure and Lebesgue-integral API.

items.name: Weak* compactness for probability measures on a compact set
items.statement: The set of Borel probability measures on a compact metric space is compact in the weak* topology, so every sequence has a convergent subsequence; used in the proof of Theorem 5.11 to extract a limit of the measures µ_N.
items.note: This is Prokhorov's theorem, or the Banach–Alaoglu theorem via the Riesz representation theorem. Mathlib has Banach–Alaoglu and the Riesz representation theorem, and the Tau Ceti optimal-transport roadmap plans weak convergence and compactness of probability measures in layer 1; ArithmeticStatistics ST.0 plans the measure-theoretic framework for equidistribution.

items.name: Minkowski's convex-body and successive-minima theorems
items.statement: Blichfeldt's lemma and Minkowski's first and second theorems for a lattice and a symmetric convex body, relating the successive minima to the covolume.
items.locator: arXiv:2111.12660v2 (16 March 2024), §3, pp. 12–16, behind Theorem 3.2 and Proposition 3.4
items.note: GeometryOfNumbersAndQuadraticArithmetic GN.1 plans exactly this: 'Prove Blichfeldt and Minkowski first/second theorems with measurable convex symmetric bodies and boundary conventions'. What is not planned there is the flatness theorem and the evaluation-polytope form the paper needs, which are routed to that layer as items of their own.

items.name: Honda–Tate theory
items.statement: The classification of isogeny classes of simple abelian varieties over a finite field F_q by conjugacy classes of Weil q-numbers, together with Tate's theorem computing Hom groups and endomorphism algebras through ℓ-adic Tate modules.
items.locator: arXiv:2111.12660v2 (16 March 2024), §5, p. 3 and Proposition 5.12, p. 40, quoting Honda–Tate
items.note: This is what converts the question of extreme point counts into an optimisation problem over measures on [−2√q, 2√q]. The atlas has no layer on abelian varieties over finite fields: a text search of every stage description for 'Honda–Tate' and 'abelian varieties over finite fields' returns nothing, and 'Weil number' returns only the weight-theoretic layers DWP.10 and R34.1. The closest owner is FaltingsFinitenessAndIsogenyTheorems R28.4, which already plans Tate's isogeny theorem and the endomorphism algebra and already imports the finite-field weight bounds.

items.name: The Weil bound for abelian varieties over finite fields
items.statement: For a simple abelian variety over F_q the eigenvalues of Frobenius are Weil q-numbers, algebraic integers all of whose archimedean absolute values equal √q; for the real ones this places the conjugates in [−2√q, 2√q].
items.note: WeightsInEtaleCohomology R34.1 plans 'Frobenius, algebraicity and weights' and R34.2 the curve and abelian-variety case, and DeligneWeightsAndPurity DWP.1 plans the initial Weil estimate for curves and abelian varieties. These supply the interval Σ in which the conjugates lie.

items.name: Upper semicontinuity of log|Q| and Serre's implication
items.statement: For a nonzero integer polynomial Q the function log|Q| is upper semicontinuous on a compact Σ ⊂ ℝ, so for a weak*-convergent sequence of counting measures µ_{R_k} → µ one has ∫_Σ log|Q| dµ ≥ limsup_k ∫_Σ log|Q| dµ_{R_k} = limsup_k log|res(R_k,Q)|/deg R_k ≥ 0.
items.note: The easy implication (2) ⇒ (1) of Theorem 1.5, recorded here because it is the statement that identifies the resultant obstruction as the only one. It is elementary but has no owner in the atlas, and travels with the potential-theoretic items.

items.name: The equilibrium measure of a finite union of intervals
items.statement: If Σ = [x₁,y₁] ∪ ⋯ ∪ [x_k,y_k] with x₁ < y₁ < ⋯ < x_k < y_k, then the unweighted equilibrium measure has dµ_Σ(t) = |P(t)| dt ∏_{i≤k}|t − x_i|^{-1/2}|t − y_i|^{-1/2} on Σ for some polynomial P; in particular µ_Σ is 1/2-Hölder. For a single interval [a,b] this is the arcsine law dx/(π√((b−x)(x−a))).
items.locator: arXiv:2111.12660v2 (16 March 2024), Remark 5.6, p. 35, and Example 5.16, p. 43
items.note: Needed so that sweetening preserves the Hölder condition. Like the rest of potential theory, it has no owner in the atlas.

prerequisites.citation: Edward B. Saff and Vilmos Totik, Logarithmic Potentials with External Fields, Grundlehren 316, Springer, 1997
prerequisites.why: The standard reference for weighted potential theory, cited as [24] for the principle of domination (I.1.4), the equilibrium measure of an interval (Example I.3.5), the weak* compactness used in Theorem 5.11 (Theorem 0.1.3) and the semicontinuity argument (0.1.2), and for balayage (Theorem II.4.4), which the paper names as the natural way to produce measures satisfying Proposition 5.15 with several auxiliary polynomials.

prerequisites.citation: Thomas Ransford, Potential Theory in the Complex Plane, LMS Student Texts 28, Cambridge, 1995
prerequisites.why: The source, cited as [22], for the definition of capacity as the supremum of e^{−I(µ)} and for the existence and uniqueness of the unweighted equilibrium measure of a compact set of positive capacity.

prerequisites.citation: M. Fekete and G. Szegő, On algebraic equations with integral coefficients whose roots belong to a given point set, Math. Z. 63 (1955), 158–172
prerequisites.why: Theorem D there is the coefficient-adjustment idea that Lemma 4.5 follows, and their paper is the progress the author names towards the complex case of Theorem 1.5.

prerequisites.citation: Raphael M. Robinson, Conjugate algebraic integers in real point sets, Math. Z. 84 (1964), 415–427
prerequisites.why: The coefficient-adjustment technique of §4 and the proof that a real set of capacity greater than 1 contains infinitely many complete sets of conjugate algebraic integers; Proposition 4.1 follows Robinson's approach, and the capacity-1 case of Theorem 1.5 is known only in the special cases he treated.

prerequisites.citation: Christopher J. Smyth, The mean values of totally real algebraic integers, Math. Comp. 42 (1984), 663–681, and Totally positive algebraic integers of small trace, Ann. Inst. Fourier 34 (1984), 1–28
prerequisites.why: The auxiliary-polynomial method and the bound λ_SSS ≥ 1.7719 that the whole subject builds on; the counting measure µ_P is taken from the first of these papers. Smyth's later note An inequality for polynomials (1999) is where he suggests that 2 may not be the smallest limit point, the reading this paper vindicates.

prerequisites.citation: Jean-Pierre Serre, Distribution asymptotique des valeurs propres des endomorphismes de Frobenius (d'après Abel, Chebyshev, Robinson, …), Séminaire Bourbaki 1146, Astérisque 414 (2019), and his letter to Christopher Smyth of 31 March 1998
prerequisites.why: The framework of limits of conjugate distributions in which Theorem 1.5 is stated, and Lemma 1.3.4 there is the easy implication (2) ⇒ (1). The 1998 letter, reproduced as Appendix B of Aguirre and Peral, contains the two-part integration argument and the optimal parameters that Example 5.16 repackages and rounds.

prerequisites.citation: Julián Aguirre and Juan Carlos Peral, The trace problem for totally positive algebraic integers, in Number Theory and Polynomials, LMS Lecture Note Ser. 352, Cambridge, 2008, 1–19, with an appendix by Jean-Pierre Serre
prerequisites.why: The detailed history of the trace problem, and the appendix containing Serre's bound: no auxiliary-polynomial inequality can hold for λ greater than 1.89830…, which together with Theorem 5.11 gives Theorem 1.1. The numbered equations (8), (10) and (11) of that appendix are used in Example 5.16.

prerequisites.citation: Issai Schur, Über die Verteilung der Wurzeln bei gewissen algebraischen Gleichungen mit ganzzahligen Koeffizienten, Math. Z. 1 (1918), 377–402; Carl Ludwig Siegel, The trace of totally positive and real algebraic integers, Ann. of Math. 46 (1945), 302–312
prerequisites.why: The original bounds e^{1/2} ≤ λ_SSS ≤ 2 and the improvement to 1.7336…, the starting point of the whole problem.

prerequisites.citation: Cong Wang, Jie Wu and Qiang Wu, Totally positive algebraic integers with small trace, Math. Comp. 90 (2021), 2317–2332
prerequisites.why: The state of the art before this paper: an auxiliary-polynomial inequality with λ = 1.793145 and 130 polynomials, and the list of the fourteen totally positive algebraic integers with trace ratio at most 1.793 that Proposition 5.17 uses to show Serre's measure is not optimal.

prerequisites.citation: Taira Honda, Isogeny classes of abelian varieties over finite fields, J. Math. Soc. Japan 20 (1968), 83–95, together with Tate's theorems on endomorphisms of abelian varieties over finite fields
prerequisites.why: Honda–Tate theory, which reduces extreme point counts for abelian varieties over F_q to an optimisation problem over measures on [−2√q, 2√q]. Nothing in the atlas covers it.

prerequisites.citation: Wojciech Banaszczyk, Alexander E. Litvak, Alain Pajor and Stanislaw J. Szarek, The flatness theorem for nonsymmetric convex bodies via the local theory of Banach spaces, Math. Oper. Res. 24 (1999), 728–750; Peter M. Gruber, Convex and Discrete Geometry, Grundlehren 336, Springer, 2007
prerequisites.why: The flatness theorem and the convex-geometry background behind Theorem 3.2 and Proposition 3.4. GeometryOfNumbersAndQuadraticArithmetic GN.1 plans Minkowski's theorems but not the flatness theorem.

prerequisites.citation: Borys Kadets, Estimates for the number of rational points on simple abelian varieties over finite fields, Math. Z. 297 (2021), 465–473; Raymond van Bommel, Edgar Costa, Wanlin Li, Bjorn Poonen and Alexander Smith, Abelian varieties of prescribed order over finite fields, arXiv:2106.13651
prerequisites.why: The previous records for extreme point counts that Corollary 1.3 improves, and the source of Construction 7.3, the coefficient-adjustment idea underlying Lemma 4.5, and of the congruence argument of Remark 5.14 making the families geometrically simple and ordinary.

prerequisites.citation: Franz Peherstorfer, Gauss–Tchebycheff quadrature formulas, Numer. Math. 58 (1990), 273–286
prerequisites.why: Lemma 2.2 there gives the explicit density of the unweighted equilibrium measure of a finite union of intervals, which Remark 5.6 uses to see that sweetening preserves the Hölder condition.

prerequisites.citation: Jacob S. Christiansen, Barry Simon and Maxim Zinchenko, Asymptotics of Chebyshev polynomials I: subsets of ℝ, Invent. Math. 208 (2017), 217–245; Vilmos Totik, Chebyshev constants and the inheritance problem, J. Approx. Theory 160 (2009), 187–201; Harold Widom, Extremal polynomials associated with a system of curves in the complex plane, Adv. Math. 3 (1969), 127–232
prerequisites.why: The theory of Chebyshev polynomials of a compact subset of ℝ and the two-sided bound C^{-1}κ^r ≤ ‖T_r‖_Σ ≤ Cκ^r of Lemma 4.2, which is where the capacity enters the construction of §4.

routes.title: Logarithmic potential theory and the distribution of conjugates of algebraic integers
routes.brief: Plan logarithmic potential theory on compact subsets of the real line and its application to the distribution of conjugates of algebraic integers, following Alexander Smith, Annals of Mathematics 200 (2024), no. 1. The final theorems are these. (1) The main theorem (Theorem 1.5): for Σ ⊂ ℝ compact with at most countably many connected components and capacity strictly greater than 1, and µ a Borel probability measure on Σ, the condition that ∫_Σ log|Q| dµ ≥ 0 for every nonzero integer polynomial Q is equivalent to the existence of infinitely many distinct irreducible monic integer polynomials R_k with all roots in Σ whose counting measures converge weak* to µ; that is, the integrality of resultants is the only obstruction to realising a measure as a limit of conjugate distributions. (2) Smyth's method is optimal (Theorem 5.11): for Σ and a continuous F with the stated growth condition, the liminf λ(Σ, F) of the mean values of F over the conjugates of algebraic integers with all conjugates in Σ equals λ_Smyth(Σ, F), the supremum of the λ admitting an auxiliary-polynomial inequality F(x) ≥ λ + Σ a_i log|Q_i(x)| on Σ. (3) The Schur–Siegel–Smyth constant satisfies λ_SSS < 1.89831 (Theorem 1.1), so there are infinitely many totally positive algebraic integers of trace less than 1.89831 times their degree and the long-standing expectation λ_SSS = 2 is false. Cover, in layers: the logarithmic potential U^µ(z) = ∫ −log|z−w| dµ(w), the energy I(µ), the capacity of a compact set and its unweighted equilibrium measure, with the Frostman inequality and the explicit equilibrium measures of an interval and of a finite union of intervals; Hölder measures, the continuity of their potentials, and the layer-cake identity that proves it; the weight w_µ = exp(U^µ) and the weighted supremum norms ‖w_µ^n P‖_Σ, with the criterion that ‖w_µ^{deg P_n}P_n‖^{1/deg P_n} → 1 forces weak* convergence of the counting measures; the approximating polynomial of a measure and the estimates relating its Vandermonde determinant to the energy; Chebyshev polynomials of a compact set with their equioscillation characterisation and the identification of lim ‖T_r‖^{1/r} with the capacity; the coefficient-adjustment technique of Robinson and of Fekete and Szegő, pruned and complementary polynomials, and the resulting construction of real monic polynomials with a long block of even integral coefficients and well-separated roots in Σ; the smoothing measures ν_{[a,b]} with their potentials, convolution smoothing and the sweetening construction that restores admissibility; the nonpositivity of the energy of an admissible measure; and finally the optimisation constants λ(Σ, F) and λ_Smyth(Σ, F), Serre's measure and the proof of Theorem 1.1, the criterion of Proposition 5.15 for certifying a candidate measure, and the obstruction of Proposition 5.17 showing that no fixed finite set of auxiliary polynomials can reach the optimum.
